howItWorks.readLead1: We check what a US dollar really costs in {n} countries, every hour.
howItWorks.readBody1: Every country has an official exchange rate. In some places you can't actually buy a dollar at that rate. We find what people really pay and show how far it is from the official rate.
howItWorks.readLead2: In {country}, a dollar costs {street} {unit}. The official rate says {rate}.
howItWorks.readBody2: So for 100 dollars, people there pay {street100} {unit} instead of {rate100}. That's {pct}% more than the official rate, so {country} shows +{pct}%. Most countries sit near 0%, which means the official rate is the real one. A minus means people pay a little less.
howItWorks.readLead3: The price comes from stablecoins, digital coins that are always worth one US dollar.
howItWorks.readBody3: People buy them with local money, so their price is the price of a dollar. We take it from local exchanges first, then brokers, then offers people post to each other on Binance and OKX. If there aren't enough offers, that country shows no price for the hour. We never guess.
howItWorks.readLead4: On {routes} routes we also check what it costs to send money abroad.
howItWorks.readBody4: We compare transfer apps with sending it by stablecoin. The cost is how much less the person receiving gets than at the official rate, with every fee we can see included. This hour, sending {amount} to the Philippines costs {cost} with {app}, the cheapest app. Where a fee can't be seen, the route says so.
howItWorks.introLead: Every hour we collect prices from {sources} public sources.
howItWorks.introRest: From them we work out two kinds of number. This page explains both, and how to check them.
howItWorks.pctLead: +{pct}% means people in {country} pay {pct}% more for a dollar than the official rate.
howItWorks.pctBody: The official rate is {rate} {unit} for a dollar. People actually pay {street}.
howItWorks.fromLead: First choice is the exchanges where people in that country buy stablecoins.
howItWorks.fromFirst: With two or more, we use the middle of their prices. With none, we use brokers. With no broker either, we use people selling to each other on Binance and OKX, and take the middle of the {minAds} cheapest. If none of those has enough, the country gets no price that hour. You see a blank, never a guess.
howItWorks.costLead: Each cost on the Routes page is what the person receiving loses compared with the official rate, with every fee we can measure included. Where one is missing, the route says so.
howItWorks.costBody: Sending {amount} to the Philippines costs {cost} with {app} this hour.

howItWorks.checkBody: A missed hour shows as a blank, never filled in.

howItWorks.pctStable: What people pay comes from stablecoins, digital coins that are each worth one US dollar. People buy them with local money, so their price shows what a dollar really costs there.
howItWorks.measureBody: Every country has an official exchange rate. In some countries banks won’t sell dollars at that rate, or sell very few, so people buy them from each other and pay more. Every hour we check what people really pay for a dollar in {n} countries and compare it with the official rate.

howItWorks.meaningZero: 0% means people pay the official rate, and most countries are close to it. A minus means they pay a little less.
howItWorks.sourceBody: We get it from local exchanges first, then brokers, then people selling to each other on Binance and OKX. What they sell is mostly stablecoins, digital coins that are always worth one US dollar, so their price is the price of a dollar. If there aren’t enough prices in an hour, that country shows no price. We never guess.

howItWorks.dollarCostTitle: A dollar's price is the middle of real offers, every hour
howItWorks.dollarCostLead: Each country gets one price for a dollar every hour, built like this.
dollarCostPoints: A stablecoin is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
We take the {minAds} cheapest offers to sell one on the exchange people there use. The middle offer is the price, so one odd seller cannot move it.
We set that price against the official rate at the same moment. The percentage is how much more a dollar really costs than that rate says.
A positive percentage means people pay more than the official rate. A negative one means they pay less.
With fewer than {minAds} sellers we publish no price. You see a blank, never a guess.
howItWorks.sendingCostTitle: Sending cost is the money lost against the official rate
howItWorks.sendingCostLead: We price each app and the stablecoin way at {amounts} amounts, with the exchange fees and the fee for moving the coin counted. Look at the one closest to what you send.
howItWorks.sendingCostAmounts: The amounts are {amountList}, in the currency you send from.
sendingCostPoints: The official rate is the rate banks use with each other.
Whatever your recipient gets below that rate is what sending costs you.
howItWorks.notMeasuredTitle: Some costs are not in our figures, so check these yourself
notMeasured: The official rate updates only once a day. On days a currency moves fast, the gap we show can be a day behind.

Money moves into an exchange and out again through a bank, a wallet or the exchange's local partner. Each has its own charge. Some show it as a fee, some bake it into the rate, some set it in a deal with the exchange. We can't see these, so they are left out.
Some app prices are offers for a first transfer. Repeat customers pay more.
Cash dollar prices come from public websites that track money changers, not from offers we read ourselves. Where we have one, the country page shows it beside the stablecoin price.

tape.title: What people pay for a dollar, updating every {minutes} minutes
tape.lede: Each row shows what people pay, the official rate, and the difference. Prices are in each country's own currency per US dollar, marked by its three letter code, such as AFN for the Afghan afghani. Central Africa and West Africa are groups of countries that share one currency. The difference is how much more people pay than the official rate, as a percentage. A minus sign means they pay less.

tape.note: A stablecoin is a digital token built to hold the value of a US dollar. What people pay comes from offers on Binance, a large online marketplace where people trade stablecoins. We line up the offers to sell a digital dollar from lowest to highest and take the one in the middle, so a few odd offers do not move the price. We compare it with the official rate, which is the bank exchange rate at the same moment. Stablecoins can be swapped for cash dollars at close to one for one, so their price is a good guide to what a dollar costs on the street. Cash prices can differ a little. If people pay more than the official rate, a dollar is hard to get at the bank price.

findingData.evidenceBasis_exchange_vs_p2p: Each row is one country: the typical gap, the share of hours with a gap of 2% or more, the hours checked, and whether the gap is still there.
findingData.method_exchange_vs_p2p: We take every hour in which a country's published price came from exchanges or brokers, and at least one board where people sell to each other had ten or more buy ads. The gap is that board's price over the official rate, minus the price we published that hour. When two boards answered we use the middle of the two. A gap is still there when, over the last 30 days, there are at least seven days of checked hours and the gap is 2% or more in at least three quarters of them.
findingData.limits_exchange_vs_p2p: Offers from people selling to each other are prices asked, not trades done. Buying on an exchange needs an account there. Binance's board was first checked on 2 Sep and OKX's on 3 Oct.

findingData.unit_weekend_increases: Saturday price rises that came back down by the Tuesday after
findingData.unit_sgd_per_month: Singapore dollars sent per month in total. Above it, stablecoins cost less for a transfer of five thousand to the Philippines.
findingData.title_price_changes: Transfer apps keep changing their prices
findingData.claim_price_changes: Transfer apps raise and cut what they charge to send money. The cheapest app when you compare may not be the cheapest when you send.
findingData.evidenceBasis_price_changes: Each row is one route: its confirmed changes, how many were rises or cuts, and how many apps moved.
findingData.method_price_changes: We record each app's cost every hour, for each amount sent, against the official rate. A change counts only when one app's daily cost moved against every other app on the same route. It must move the same way, on the same day, by more than a small set amount. Moves that every app shares come from the exchange rate and never count. Each day needs several hourly readings, and a day is judged only once it has ended.
findingData.limits_price_changes: Each amount sent counts on its own. An app that changes its price at several amounts counts once for each. The number does not say how big any change was. It covers only the routes and apps we check, from the day each was added.
findingData.title_weekend_penalty: Some apps charge more on Saturday, then cut back
findingData.claim_weekend_penalty: A rise counts when an app charged more on a Saturday and came back down by Tuesday. If your transfer can wait, a weekday can cost less.
findingData.evidenceBasis_weekend_penalty: Each row is one route: its Saturday rises that came back, the cuts that undid them, and how many Saturdays we checked.
findingData.method_weekend_penalty: We start from the confirmed price changes. A rise counts when an app raised its price on a Saturday. The same app must then cut its price on the same route by the Tuesday after. Both moves must be in our data. We never assume a return from the rise alone.
findingData.limits_weekend_penalty: A rise counts once, however many amounts it showed up at. The number does not say how much more a Saturday cost. A route with few Saturdays checked has had little chance to show this.
findingData.title_volume_crossover: From Singapore to the Philippines, a stablecoin only beats the apps if you send over {approx} a month
findingData.claim_volume_crossover: Sending S$5,000 to the Philippines, a stablecoin would only beat the cheapest app if you sent more than this every month, because exchanges cut their fees for big traders. Nobody in our data traded that much, so this is worked out from the fees the exchanges publish, not seen happening. A stablecoin is a coin that stays worth one US dollar.
findingData.evidenceBasis_volume_crossover: Both rows are the same transfer, priced for two ways of buying on the exchange. Costs are for sending S$5,000.
findingData.method_volume_crossover: We take every real check of sending five thousand Singapore dollars to the Philippines by stablecoin. For a given monthly volume, we look up the lower fee each exchange would charge. We rebuild each check's cost with those fees, from its own recorded prices. The number is the lowest volume where its usual cost drops below the cheapest app's usual cost. Both come from the same hours.
findingData.limits_volume_crossover: It covers one route and one amount. The number is rebuilt from real prices, never seen happening. Nobody in our data traded at that volume. It does not mean stablecoins are cheaper for most senders. Below that volume, the cheapest app costs less for this transfer.
findingData.limits_sgd_php_never_cheapest: It covers one route and only the hours we priced. It does not say a stablecoin can never win: on other routes it was the cheapest in some hours, and this route may change.
findingData.method_sgd_php_never_cheapest: Every hour we price the stablecoin way and each app for this route. A stablecoin counts as cheapest when its cost is below every app's cost in that hour. The count is the same one the home page and the routes page print.
findingData.evidenceBasis_sgd_php_never_cheapest: Each row is one amount sent from Singapore to the Philippines: the hours we priced, and the hours in which a stablecoin was cheapest.
